A.explanation: This correctly describes the motion because with no air resistance there is no horizontal acceleration, so $v_x = u\cos\theta$ stays constant.

B.explanation: This correctly describes the motion because range equals constant horizontal velocity multiplied by total flight time, $x = u\cos\theta \times t$.

C.explanation: This correctly describes the motion because the trajectory is symmetric, so maximum height is reached halfway through the total flight time $t$.

D.explanation: This does not describe the motion because gravity accelerates the object vertically, so $u\sin\theta$ is only the initial vertical velocity, not a constant value.

hints: Notice the launch velocity $u$ at angle $\theta$ in the diagram must be resolved into $u\cos\theta$ horizontally and $u\sin\theta$ vertically.
Connect this to negligible air resistance: zero horizontal force means zero horizontal acceleration, but weight still gives a constant downward vertical acceleration $g$.
Compare each statement against that difference and check the symmetry of flight time $t$ and range $tu\cos\theta$ to spot the one statement about a constant vertical velocity.
walkthrough: Resolve the initial velocity from the diagram: horizontal component $v_x = u\cos\theta$ and initial vertical component $v_{y0} = u\sin\theta$.
Apply Newton's laws with air resistance negligible: no horizontal force so horizontal acceleration is zero and $v_x$ remains $u\cos\theta$ throughout flight.
Calculate horizontal displacement as constant velocity multiplied by time: $x = v_x t = tu\cos\theta$.
Use vertical symmetry: the object rises to zero vertical velocity at maximum height then falls back to the ground, so time up equals time down and time to maximum height is $t/2$.
Check the vertical velocity: weight causes constant downward acceleration, so $v_y = u\sin\theta - gt$ decreases continuously and is not constant.
Therefore the statement claiming the vertical component is constant at $u\sin\theta$ does not describe the motion. This is option D.
